title: The Parable of the Three Rings
text:
In Boccaccio's Decameron, Saladin, the sultan of Egypt, needed money and summoned Melchizedek, a wealthy Jewish moneylender of Alexandria. Hoping to trap him, he asked which of the three laws was the true one: the Jewish, the Muslim or the Christian.

Melchizedek saw the danger and answered with a story. A rich man once owned a beautiful and precious ring and declared that whichever son received it would be his heir and head of the family. The ring passed down through generations until it came to a father who loved his three sons equally and could not choose among them. He secretly had a master craftsman make two copies so perfect that even he could not tell them apart, and before he died he gave each son a ring in private.

After his death each son claimed the inheritance and produced his ring. The rings were identical, and the question of which was the true heir, said Melchizedek, is still pending. So it is with the three laws given by God to three peoples.

Saladin saw how skillfully he had escaped the snare, told him openly what he needed, and Melchizedek lent the money. Saladin repaid it in full, honored him with gifts and kept him as a friend. Four centuries later Lessing retold the parable in Nathan the Wise, adding a judge who tells each son to prove his ring by the goodness of his life.
lesson: When people disagree on questions no one can settle, respect and good conduct do more than winning the argument. Let your actions make your case.
location: Florence (modern Italy); set in Alexandria and Cairo (modern Egypt)
source: Giovanni Boccaccio, Decameron, Day 1, Story 3; Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Nathan the Wise (1779), Act III
